title: Sawpit Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Sawpit wells have a 126-foot median depth, 10 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $14,200-$24,600.
h1: Sawpit, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Well records within 5 miles of Sawpit show a mountain drilling area dominated by fractured-bedrock wells. Of 667 wells in Colorado DWR permit records, 390 are recorded as constructed, 425 report total depth, and 151 report a pump yield. That is useful local evidence, but it is not a guarantee for a particular lot. Ground conditions can change across short distances in granite and gneiss.

For a buyer, the main local benchmarks are a 126-foot median depth and a 10.0 gpm median yield. The records also show many shallow wells, but some extend much deeper. Check the permits and completion reports for nearby parcels before relying on a seller's estimate or a drilling bid.

sections.heading: Sawpit well depth depends on fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
The median permitted well near Sawpit is 126 feet deep. The middle half runs from 45 to 300 feet, so a driller bidding a new well needs to allow for a wide range rather than treating the median as a guaranteed target. About 44% of recorded wells are under 100 feet, while 31% fall between 100 and 300 feet.

Deeper drilling is common enough to affect planning: 22% are between 300 and 600 feet, 4% are above 600 feet, and the deepest record reaches 1,200 feet. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer. Granite and gneiss can produce water through fractures, which makes neighboring well depths a useful guide but not a promise.

sections.heading: Water yield near Sawpit is usually workable, not uniform
sections.html:
The reported pump-yield median is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.0 and 13.0 gpm. Most reported wells, 60%, produce between 5 and 15 gpm. Another 21% report more than 15 gpm. Those figures suggest that a typical domestic well can be productive, but the spread matters when sizing storage and planning a larger home.

Low-yield records are present but not dominant. 1% report under 1 gpm, and 17% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. Only 151 wells report a pump yield, so the statistics describe the reporting subset. Ask for the well test, production rate, storage setup, and recovery information before assuming a parcel can support household demand.

sections.heading: Sawpit water levels look stable in the available records
sections.html:
Among the 40 wells reporting static water levels, the median depth to water is 54 feet below the surface. The middle half ranges from 23 to 166 feet, a substantial spread for pump sizing and trench planning. A shallow water level does not by itself prove a high-producing well; yield and water level measure different parts of the well's performance.

The decade comparison does not show a meaningful drop in the recorded median. Measurements from the 2010s have a median of 53 feet, compared with 54 feet in the 2020s. That is a limited dataset, not a basin-wide guarantee. Have the seller provide the well construction and water-level records for the exact property, then compare them with nearby permits.

sections.heading: Sawpit permits show long drilling activity and current records
sections.html:
Permit activity near Sawpit extends back to the 1960s, when 2 permits were issued. Activity increased to 56 in the 1970s, 85 in the 1980s, and 187 in the 1990s. The records show 151 permits in the 2000s, 56 in the 2010s, and 39 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most active named drillers in these records are Valley Drilling Co. (Stoy, Kenneth), with 84 records; Western Drilling Services, LLC (Kuchler, Richard A.), with 75; and Bill Kissner Drilling Inc. (Kissner, Bill F.), with 60. These are permit-record counts, not endorsements or proof of current availability.

sections.heading: What a new Sawpit well may cost to drill
sections.html:
Sawpit's fractured mountain bedrock is the main cost variable. A local planning model uses a drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the 126-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $8,200 to $12,600. That is only the drilling portion and should not be mistaken for the complete water system.

Including a pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, the estimated finished-well range at the median depth is $14,200 to $24,600. A 300-foot well, a difficult access route, deeper casing, or extra site work can change the bid. Get the contractor to state what is included, how failed or dry-hole footage is handled, and whether permitting, testing, casing, grout, and connection work are separate charges.

sections.heading: Risks to check before buying or building near Sawpit
sections.html:
Low yield and dry-hole risk deserve attention because fractured rock does not distribute water evenly. Although only 1% of reported yields are under 1 gpm, another 17% are between 1 and 5 gpm, and the yield dataset covers just 151 wells. A neighboring high-producing well is encouraging, but it cannot guarantee the same fracture system on your lot.

Environmental review also matters. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 130 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. That does not establish contamination at a specific property. Test the existing well, review mine and PFAS information, and confirm septic setbacks, drainfield space, access for drilling equipment, and the building location before closing.

sections.heading: Use nearby permits to plan a Sawpit lot
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then compare its records with wells around Placerville, about 2 miles away, and other nearby areas such as Mountain Village, Telluride, Ophir, Ridgway, and Portland. Look for depth, named aquifer, static water level, yield test, casing, and construction details rather than relying on a single nearby well. DWR permit status and completion records should be part of the purchase file.

For a new build, budget around the local depth and cost ranges while keeping room for deeper fractured rock. Confirm the proposed well location, septic layout, driveway access, electrical route, and storage needs together. An exempt household-use well still has state rules, including the 35 gpm pumping limit. In an over-appropriated basin, confirm whether an augmentation plan is required before depending on the well for the intended use.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Sawpit, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth within 5 miles of Sawpit is 126 feet. The middle half runs from 45 to 300 feet. About 44% are under 100 feet, but the deepest recorded well reaches 1,200 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make nearby completion records useful for planning, not a guarantee of depth on a new lot.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Sawpit?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 126-foot median depth, drilling is estimated at $8,200 to $12,600. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $14,200 to $24,600. A deeper hole, difficult access, or additional site work can raise the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Sawpit?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 10.0 gpm, with the middle half between 5.0 and 13.0 gpm. About 60% report 5 to 15 gpm, while 17% report 1 to 5 gpm. Only 151 wells report yield, so review the exact property's test and storage capacity before planning household demand.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Sawpit?
faq.a: The well records do not establish drinking-water safety. Within about 10 miles are 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 130 historic mine features, and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Have the well tested by a qualified laboratory, review nearby environmental history, and test again after construction or repairs before using the water for drinking.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping near Sawpit?
faq.a: The available records do not show a clear decline in median static water level. The median was 53 feet below surface in the 2010s and 54 feet in the 2020s. However, only 40 wells report static water levels, and the middle half spans 23 to 166 feet. Treat the trend as limited local evidence, not a guarantee.
